deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivation, formula or computation. It is a programmatic, methodological note in Hilbert's notebook. It continues the previous page's argument about physics and existence proofs, which used the Neumann–Schwarz solvability of the boundary-value problem for heat conduction. The page has three parts.

(1) Characterisation of modern mathematics. The key feature of modern mathematics, which will become ever clearer in the future, is the wish to 'understand inwardly'. Earlier, discoveries came from formal processes that now look like lucky accidents. That mode is now 'entirely excluded': one 'wades in sand' and feels miserable doing mere calculation ('Rechnerei') while waiting for a lucky chance. Today the idea is the main thing: an idea that can be described in words, governs the connections between results, and supplies our intuition ('Anschauung'). The beginnings are placed in Riemann's function theory, then number theory, then differential equations (Lie etc.). The summit ('Gipfel') is the axiomatic method. It systematically eliminates guessing, i.e. the lucky accident, because all combinations, that is all logically compatible systems of assumptions, are taken into account. The task is then to order all the available material from the standpoint of the axiomatic method.

(2) What the physicist needs for real progress in physics:
- mathematical treatment of special problems;
- a short, comprehensive overview of the whole of physical theory and its interconnections in mathematical dress, i.e. by means of concise ('prägnante') expressions;
- a survey of the consequences of hypotheses, e.g. electron theory.

(3) What physics needs for a satisfactory logical foundation. Hilbert asks whether a physicist is right to say that two results do not interest him and have no significance for physics:
- (a) the proof of existence of a solution of the boundary-value problem;
- (b) the theorem that an arbitrary function can be expanded in eigenfunctions.
Hilbert's answer is that such a physicist is 'completely wrong'. Per the previous page, his reason is that these theorems establish the consistency (Widerspruchslosigkeit) of the physical axioms with the simplest observed facts, such as the existence of thermal equilibrium.

There are no implicit mathematical steps to fill in.

results.what: The axiomatic method presented as the culmination of 'conceptual' modern mathematics: systematic consideration of all logically compatible systems of assumptions, replacing calculation and lucky guessing.
results.modern_name: Hilbert's axiomatic method / conceptual (Riemannian) style of mathematics
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert (Grundlagen der Geometrie 1899, 'Axiomatisches Denken' 1917/18; Riemann/Dirichlet tradition of 'thinking in concepts')

results.what: Programme of what physics needs from mathematics: treatment of special problems, unified concise mathematical overview of theories, and derivation of consequences of hypotheses (e.g. electron theory).
results.modern_name: Hilbert's programme of axiomatization of physics (6th Problem)
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert (1900 Paris problems, lectures on physics 1905 onward; analysed by L. Corry)

results.what: Claim that existence theorems for boundary-value problems and expansion theorems in eigenfunctions are physically essential, because they secure the consistency of the physical axioms.
results.modern_name: Physical significance of existence theorems (Dirichlet problem) and spectral/eigenfunction expansion theorems
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (Dirichlet principle 1899/1904; integral equations 1904–1910); the existence proofs themselves go back to Schwarz and C. Neumann

deep.surprise_reason: These are well-documented Hilbertian views: the primacy of conceptual over computational mathematics, the axiomatic method as its summit, axiomatization of physics, and the importance of existence and eigenfunction-expansion theorems for physics. They are expressed in his published lectures and addresses and discussed by Corry and others using these same notebooks (Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600). The page contains no new mathematics.
